name: cr_017
user_goal: Here's my story I want to process: When Claire Delacroix was eleven years old, her mother married into the Havenwood family, and Claire was taken to live in a house she would grow to hate. Havenwood was a tall gray Victorian on a Louisiana bayou, built by a family of cane planters in 1871, with wrought-iron galleries, shuttered rooms, and a long history of quiet dying. The housekeeper, Mrs. Peltier, had served three generations of Havenwoods; she liked Claire's mother and disliked Claire, who was thin and serious and watchful and had not yet learned to pretend at affection. Claire's stepfather, Bernard Havenwood, had three daughters of his own from his first marriage. The eldest was named Odette. The middle was Marguerite. The youngest, only five years old, was called Lenore. Claire was given a room in the east wing, which the Havenwood daughters had never used because, Odette told her on her first night, that wing was the cold one. Claire did not know what this meant until her first week in the house, when a dress her mother had packed for her disappeared from her wardrobe and reappeared, ten minutes later, neatly folded on her pillow. Claire was not frightened. She was eleven years old and she was a careful child and she decided, that night, to begin keeping a notebook. By the end of her first year at Havenwood, Claire had filled two notebooks. She had seen a young woman in a violet dress standing at the end of the second-floor corridor on three separate nights, always at the same hour, always disappearing when Claire blinked. She had heard a child's laugh in the empty nursery at the end of the east wing. She had felt a cold hand brush her shoulder in the library, once, and a warmth press against her back, as if in comfort, during her first nightmare in the house. Most chillingly, she had learned from the elderly gardener that the young woman in the violet dress had lived and died in that house in 1904, and that the child in the nursery was Bernard Havenwood's first wife's first daughter, who had drowned in the bayou at the age of six, and whose body had been carried back through those very rooms. Her stepsisters denied all of it. Odette in particular mocked her for the notebooks, calling her the Ghost Girl in a way that was not kind. But Claire noticed something strange. As the years passed, the gentle ghosts of Havenwood — for she had come to think of them as such — seemed always to calm when Claire was near. Odette, by contrast, would flinch sometimes in her own house, at cold draughts, at footfalls behind her on the stairs, at a child's laugh from empty rooms. When Claire was sixteen, Bernard Havenwood, her stepfather, died suddenly in his study of a heart attack. Claire was the one who found him. The violet-dressed woman was standing behind his armchair when Claire opened the door, and she looked, for the first time, tired. Claire held the ghost's gaze for a long moment before the woman dissolved. Then Claire called her mother and Mrs. Peltier. Years later, when the will was read, Claire inherited the house. — Turn this into a Southern-Gothic haunted-mansion mini-drama, needs some haunted-mansion ambient sounds
